newsitem.title: USA: Chinese dissident Wang seeks to join Taiwan party.
newsitem.headline: Chinese dissident Wang seeks to join Taiwan party.

text.p: Chinese dissident Wang Xizhe, speaking in public for the first time since fleeing to the United States, said on Monday he would apply to join Taiwan's Nationalist Party, the Kuomintang.

"I hope the KMT (Kuomintang) leadership will consider my membership application seriously," he said. By doing so, they could show the KMT was "still a party in the whole of China, not just a party in Taiwan," Wang said.

At a crowded news conference in Oakland, near San Francisco, Wang said if the Chinese government could guarantee his safe return to China and that freedom of speech existed there, he would be willing to go back to China to face charges of illegally crossing the border to Hong Kong.

"If the Chinese authorities dare to guarantee that they will respect and observe the laws and the constitution that they enacted, then there's no ... road of no return. I will return any time," Wang said.

Wang fled his home in China's Guangdong province this month, days after authorities in Beijing arrested pro-democracy activist Liu Xiaobo and ordered him to serve three years in a labour camp. Wang went first to Hong Kong and flew via Europe to the San Francisco area last week.
Wang said he hoped U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who is due to visit China next month, would carry a letter from Wang to Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.
In the letter, Wang asked Qian to confirm a statement by a spokesman for the Chinese Foreign Ministry that Wang was not being investigated because of his political views.
"I will return to my country immediately after you make such a promise, and I am willing to be punished according to migration law that I offended," Wang wrote.

Wang, 46, one of China's leading dissidents, said through an interpreter he would not apply for political asylum in the United States until authorities in Taiwan gave him a definite answer on whether he could go there.
Wang said he hoped some day he could join the KMT delegation for negotiations with the Chinese Communist Party on unification of China and Taiwan.
If the KMT agreed to let him join, it would be their decision where he would live, Wang said. But he thought it would not be a problem to stay in the United States.

Wang, dressed in suit and tie and looking in good health, animatedly attacked Chinese leaders, accusing them of violating the country's constitution by placing the armed forces under the control of the Communist Party rather than the People's Congress.

"I don't understand the rationale that Liu should be sentenced to three years in labour camp but not (Chinese President) Jiang Zemin," he said. Wang and Liu made similar charges in a letter they wrote recently demanding Jiang be impeached.
Wang sent his love to his sick parents and his wife, saying he wanted to tell his wife: "I love her forever."

Wang said China was his homeland and he would like to stay there, but he said persecution of pro-democracy activists had reached an unreasonable level. After Liu's arrest, he said he was under close surveillance.
Friends in the United States contacted him and asked him to consider leaving China, he said. "At that time, I told them I would not leave China until the last moment."

He said he decided to hide for a short time to decide what to do when he was contacted by a friend in Hong Kong, who also urged him to leave. Wang said he decided to flee after Hong Kong television reported he was missing.

Wang's activism dates from 1974 when he co-authored an attack in Guangdong on the radical 1966-76 Cultural Revolution. He took part in the 1979 Democracy Wall movement in Beijing and produced his own dissident newsletters.
He was twice imprisoned and spent 17 years in jail and labour camps. He was released on parole in 1993.

Wang said he wanted to promote the Chinese democracy movement in the United States, to publish an English-language version of his autobiography "Toward Darkness" and to study at a higher-education institution.
